nodes.label: Agha Mohammad Khan
nodes.full: Agha Mohammad Khan, castrated as a child hostage by a rival dynasty, reunified Iran through a brutally punitive military campaign — the mass blinding of Kerman's population after the city resisted him remains one of the most infamous single episodes in modern Iranian history — before being assassinated by his own servants only months after his coronation.
nodes.src: Comparative Qajar-era chronicle sources on Agha Mohammad Khan's unification campaign.

nodes.label: Massacre of Kerman
nodes.full: After Kerman sheltered a rival claimant, Agha Mohammad Khan's forces killed or blinded a substantial portion of the city's male population and enslaved many women and children — an act of exemplary terror intended to end resistance to his unification campaign once and for all, and one still remembered as among the darkest episodes of the entire Qajar founding.
nodes.src: Comparative Qajar-era chronicle accounts of the Kerman campaign, with the customary caution that period casualty figures require critical treatment.

nodes.label: Fath-Ali Shah and Mohammad Shah
nodes.full: Fath-Ali Shah's long reign and his son Mohammad Shah's shorter one together spanned the opening decades of the 'Great Game' — the strategic rivalry between an expanding Russian Empire and British India that would shape Iranian foreign policy for the rest of the Qajar period, beginning with catastrophic territorial losses in the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Comparative early Qajar-era chronicle and diplomatic sources.

nodes.label: Russo-Persian Wars
nodes.full: Two disastrous wars against an expanding Russian Empire ended with the Treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828), stripping Iran permanently of its Caucasus territories — the South Caucasus, including Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan's northern portion — a loss of land and prestige Iranian nationalist memory would treat as a defining historical wound for generations.
nodes.src: Treaty of Gulistan (1813) and Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828), full texts.

nodes.label: Great Game across Iran
nodes.full: From the Russo-Persian Wars through the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention to the failed 1919 Anglo-Persian Agreement, Iran spent most of the Qajar period as a strategic buffer and arena for British and Russian imperial rivalry rather than a fully sovereign actor in its own right — a geopolitical position that shaped nearly every major internal Iranian political development of the era.
nodes.src: Firuz Kazemzadeh, Russia and Britain in Persia, 1864–1914 (1968).

nodes.label: Qajar royal portraiture
nodes.full: Fath-Ali Shah commissioned a distinctive style of large-scale oil portraiture — the shah shown enthroned in elaborate jewelled regalia, often with his extensive family — that fused Persian pictorial convention with European oil-painting technique introduced through growing diplomatic contact, creating an instantly recognisable Qajar royal visual identity.
nodes.src: Qajar-era royal portrait corpus, Golestan Palace collection, Tehran; Brooklyn Museum and other Western collections.

nodes.label: Golestan Palace
nodes.full: The Qajar royal complex at Tehran, built and expanded across the 19th century, combined traditional Persian architectural elements with increasingly visible European stylistic influence in its mirror halls and reception rooms — a physical record of the dynasty's gradual, uneven cultural engagement with European models throughout its history.
nodes.src: Golestan Palace, Tehran, extant complex, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2013).

nodes.label: Naser al-Din Shah
nodes.full: Iran's longest-reigning Qajar shah began with his reforming chief minister Amir Kabir's modernisation programme before having him murdered out of court jealousy, spent much of his reign granting and then cancelling controversial foreign economic concessions, and was assassinated in 1896 by a follower of the pan-Islamic reformist Jamal al-Din al-Afghani.
nodes.src: E'temad al-Saltaneh, Ruznameh-ye Khaterat (court diary), the fullest contemporary chronicle of Naser al-Din Shah's reign.

nodes.label: Amir Kabir and Dar al-Fonun
nodes.full: As chief minister to the young Naser al-Din Shah, Amir Kabir founded the Dar al-Fonun — Iran's first modern polytechnic college, teaching European sciences, languages and military techniques — alongside fiscal and administrative reforms that threatened entrenched court interests badly enough that the shah had him murdered within three years of appointing him.
nodes.src: Dar al-Fonun founding decree (1851); comparative biographical sources on Amir Kabir's reform programme.

nodes.label: Reuter and tobacco concessions
nodes.full: Naser al-Din Shah granted the British subject Baron Julius de Reuter a sweeping 1872 concession over Iran's railways, mines, and much of its economic infrastructure — cancelled within a year under domestic and Russian pressure — a pattern of granting and then retracting major foreign economic concessions that recurred throughout the later Qajar period and left the state chronically short of the revenue such deals had promised.
nodes.src: Reuter Concession text (1872); Firuz Kazemzadeh, Russia and Britain in Persia, 1864–1914 (1968).

nodes.label: Persian telegraph line
nodes.full: A telegraph line built with British technical assistance connected Tehran to the Indo-European telegraph network linking London to India, giving Iran near-instantaneous communication with the outside world for the first time — infrastructure whose diplomatic and commercial importance to British imperial interests also gave Britain new leverage inside Iran itself.
nodes.src: Indo-European Telegraph Department records on the Persian line's construction.

nodes.label: Tobacco Protest
nodes.full: A nationwide boycott of tobacco, triggered by Naser al-Din Shah's grant of a full national tobacco monopoly to a British concessionaire and enforced by a fatwa from the senior cleric Mirza Hasan Shirazi, forced the shah to cancel the concession entirely — the first successful instance of mass popular and clerical resistance compelling a Qajar shah to reverse a major policy decision.
nodes.src: Mirza Hasan Shirazi's tobacco fatwa (1891); Nikki Keddie, Religion and Rebellion in Iran: The Tobacco Protest of 1891–1892 (1966).

nodes.label: Clerical authority shown
nodes.full: Mirza Hasan Shirazi's tobacco fatwa, issued from his seminary in Samarra rather than from within Iran itself, showed that a single senior Shia jurist's religious ruling could override a shah's own economic policy nationwide — a demonstration of the ulama's independent political leverage that emboldened clerical involvement in the later Constitutional Revolution.
nodes.src: Mirza Hasan Shirazi's tobacco fatwa (1891).

nodes.label: Malkam Khan and Qanun
nodes.full: Mirza Malkam Khan's exile newspaper Qanun, smuggled into Iran from London, and a wider circle of reform-minded intellectuals and clerics argued for constitutional and legal reform grounded in both European political theory and Islamic jurisprudence — an intellectual current that directly fed the demands raised in the 1905–1911 Constitutional Revolution.
nodes.src: Mirza Malkam Khan, Qanun (newspaper, published in exile 1890–1898).

nodes.label: Mozaffar al-Din and the Constitution
nodes.full: Facing sustained mass protest and clerical pressure, Mozaffar al-Din Shah signed Iran's first constitution and authorised an elected national assembly (Majlis) just weeks before his death in January 1907 — a reluctant but historic concession that transformed Iranian politics permanently, whatever his own private reservations about it.
nodes.src: Ahmad Kasravi, Tarikh-e Mashruteh-ye Iran (History of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution).

nodes.label: First constitution
nodes.full: The 1906 Fundamental Law and its 1907 Supplement established an elected national consultative assembly (Majlis), a framework of ministerial responsibility, and a limited bill of rights — the first written constitution in Iranian history and the founding legal document of a constitutionalist political tradition that outlasted the Qajar dynasty itself.
nodes.src: The Constitution of 1906 and its Supplementary Fundamental Laws of 1907, full texts.

nodes.label: Clergy divided
nodes.full: Senior clerics split sharply over constitutionalism: figures like Akhund Khorasani in Najaf issued rulings supporting the constitutional movement as compatible with Islamic governance, while Sheikh Fazlollah Nouri argued a constitution subordinating religious law to a secular assembly was itself un-Islamic — a division within the ulama that ended when the constitutionalist restoration of 1909 had Nouri tried and publicly hanged.
nodes.src: Comparative accounts of the clerical debate over constitutionalism; Abdul-Hadi Hairi, Shi'ism and Constitutionalism in Iran (1977).

nodes.label: Mohammad Ali Shah coup
nodes.full: Mohammad Ali Shah used Russian-trained Cossack Brigade artillery to bombard and dissolve the newly elected Majlis in 1908, only to be deposed himself in 1909 when constitutionalist forces from Tabriz, Rasht and the Bakhtiari tribal confederation converged on Tehran and restored the parliament by force.
nodes.src: Ahmad Kasravi, Tarikh-e Mashruteh-ye Iran, on the 1908 coup and 1909 constitutionalist restoration.

nodes.label: Bombardment of the Majlis
nodes.full: Mohammad Ali Shah's Cossack Brigade shelled the parliament building in June 1908, killing constitutionalist deputies and journalists and suspending the constitution — provoking an armed constitutionalist resistance centred on Tabriz under Sattar Khan that, joined by forces from Rasht and Isfahan, marched on and retook Tehran in July 1909, deposing the shah.
nodes.src: Ahmad Kasravi, Tarikh-e Mashruteh-ye Iran, the principal narrative history of the Constitutional Revolution's civil war.

nodes.label: Women in the revolution
nodes.full: Women organised secret societies (anjomans) supporting the constitutional cause, ran fundraising and boycott campaigns, and in Tabriz some armed themselves to help defend the city during the 1908–09 civil war — documented political participation largely excluded from the formal citizenship rights the 1906 constitution itself granted only to men.
nodes.src: Comparative accounts of women's anjomans and the defence of Tabriz during the Constitutional Revolution.

nodes.label: Kasravi history
nodes.full: Ahmad Kasravi's Tarikh-e Mashruteh-ye Iran, written a generation after the events it describes by a participant-turned-historian, remains the single most detailed and widely used narrative source for the Constitutional Revolution — a work whose scope and level of documentary detail modern historians still rely on for the period's political history.
nodes.src: Ahmad Kasravi, Tarikh-e Mashruteh-ye Iran (History of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution).

nodes.label: D’Arcy oil concession
nodes.full: William Knox D'Arcy's 1901 concession granted him exclusive rights to Iranian oil exploration across most of the country in exchange for royalties; the discovery of commercially viable oil at Masjed Soleyman in 1908 founded what became the Anglo-Persian Oil Company — a single concession whose consequences would shape Iranian and world politics for the rest of the twentieth century.
nodes.src: D'Arcy Concession text (1901); Anglo-Persian Oil Company founding records (1909).

nodes.label: First Middle Eastern oil well
nodes.full: The well that struck oil at Masjed Soleyman in May 1908 was the first commercially productive oil well anywhere in the Middle East, using drilling technology and expertise imported directly from the already-established American and Caucasian oil industries — the technical opening chapter of what would become the region's defining industry.
nodes.src: Anglo-Persian Oil Company technical records on the Masjed Soleyman discovery well.

nodes.label: Discovery that defines the century
nodes.full: The 1908 Masjed Soleyman oil strike, made in the same turbulent year as the constitutional crisis's bombardment of the Majlis, set in motion the entire twentieth-century pattern of foreign-controlled Middle Eastern oil extraction, revenue disputes and great-power strategic interest that would shape Iranian — and regional — politics for the following hundred years.
nodes.src: Anglo-Persian Oil Company founding records (1909); comparative twentieth-century Middle East oil-politics historiography.

nodes.label: Anglo-Russian Convention
nodes.full: Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence — a Russian zone in the north, a British zone in the southeast, and a nominally neutral central zone — without any Iranian representative present at the negotiations, a stark demonstration of how little the two great powers considered Iranian sovereignty relevant to their own strategic bargaining.
nodes.src: Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, full text.

nodes.label: Occupation of neutral Iran
nodes.full: Despite declaring neutrality, Iran was invaded, occupied and fought over by Russian, British and Ottoman forces throughout the First World War, its territory used as a battleground by powers that never formally recognised its stated neutrality — a stark demonstration of how little real sovereignty the weakened Qajar state could actually enforce.
nodes.src: Comparative diplomatic and military history of Iran's occupation during the First World War.

nodes.label: Wartime famine
nodes.full: Wartime occupation, disrupted trade and requisitioned grain supplies combined with the global influenza pandemic to produce a severe famine across Iran in the final years of the First World War, with mortality estimates in the hundreds of thousands to low millions — a humanitarian catastrophe largely overshadowed in most accounts of the period by the war's political and military history.
nodes.src: Comparative demographic and famine-history scholarship on Iran's 1917–1919 wartime famine, with the customary caution that period mortality estimates vary considerably by source.

nodes.label: Anglo-Persian Agreement fails
nodes.full: A 1919 agreement that would have given Britain effective control over Iran's military and finances in exchange for loans and advisers provoked such strong nationalist and parliamentary opposition, along with American and French diplomatic objections, that the Majlis never ratified it — a rare successful Iranian resistance to a great-power arrangement during this period.
nodes.src: Anglo-Persian Agreement of 1919, full text and its failed ratification process.

nodes.label: Reza Khan coup
nodes.full: Cossack Brigade commander Reza Khan marched on Tehran with British acquiescence and installed a new government in which he held the war ministry — the opening move of a rise that would, within four years, see him depose the Qajar dynasty entirely and crown himself shah in its place.
nodes.src: British and Iranian diplomatic correspondence on the 1921 coup.

nodes.label: Ahmad Shah
nodes.full: Crowned as a child amid the constitutional restoration, Ahmad Shah presided over a weak, foreign-occupied state through the First World War and its aftermath before the Majlis, at the instigation of the rising military strongman Reza Khan, formally deposed the Qajar dynasty in 1925 and installed Reza Khan as the founder of a new ruling house.
nodes.src: Comparative late Qajar-era parliamentary and diplomatic sources, 1909–1925.

nodes.label: Siege of Herat
nodes.full: Muhammad Shah’s army besieged Herat from November 1837, a Qajar bid to recover the western Afghan city that Persian rulers regarded as part of historic Khorasan; the defence under Yar Muhammad Khan, advised by the young British officer Eldred Pottinger, held out through a failed Persian assault in June 1838. The Persians lifted the siege in September 1838 after Britain landed troops on Kharg Island and delivered an ultimatum — an early episode of the British–Russian rivalry over Iran’s eastern frontier, since Russian officers and diplomats advised the Persian side.
nodes.src: Eldred Pottinger’s narrative of the defence (in J.W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan, 1851); Sepehr, Nasikh al-Tawarikh, gives the Qajar court’s account; the extent of Russian involvement is debated.

nodes.label: Herat retaken, Anglo-Persian War
nodes.full: Persian forces took Herat in October 1856 after a siege begun in late March, in breach of an 1853 undertaking not to send troops to the city; Britain declared war on Persia the following month and landed forces at Bushehr and Khorramshahr in the Gulf. The Treaty of Paris, signed on 4 March 1857, required Persia to withdraw from Herat and “every other part of Afghanistan” and to recognise Afghan independence — fixing, for the rest of the Qajar period, Iran’s eastern limit at Herat’s doorstep.
nodes.src: Treaty of Paris between Britain and Persia, 4 March 1857; Anglo-Persian agreement of 25 January 1853 on Herat; the Persian claim to Herat rested on its earlier place in Safavid and Afsharid Khorasan.

nodes.label: Geok Tepe and the Turkmen frontier
nodes.full: Russian forces under General Mikhail Skobelev stormed the Turkmen fortress of Geok Tepe in January 1881 after a siege that began in December 1880, breaking the Akhal-Teke Turkmen who had raided Khorasan for generations and bringing Russian rule to Persia’s north-eastern border. Persia accepted the Akhal–Khorasan Convention of 1881, which fixed the frontier from the Caspian toward Baba Durmaz; commissioners completed its demarcation only in 1885.
nodes.src: Akhal–Khorasan Boundary Convention (signed 21 September 1881 according to most reference works; demarcation completed 1885); contemporary casualty estimates for the Turkmen defenders and the pursuit vary widely and are deliberately not given here.

nodes.label: Russian shelling of Imam Reza shrine
nodes.full: On 29–30 March 1912, amid unrest in Mashhad and heavy Russian pressure on Persia after the 1911 ultimatum, Russian artillery fired on the shrine of Imam Reza, where anti-Russian protesters had reportedly taken sanctuary, and Russian troops entered its precincts. Worshippers were killed and parts of the complex damaged; the shelling of the holiest Shia shrine inside Iran became a lasting emblem of Russian encroachment in the north-east.
nodes.src: British consular “Persia Diaries” for 1912 (Qatar Digital Library); W. Morgan Shuster, The Strangling of Persia (1912), on the wider Russian pressure; sources give 29 or 30 March, and casualty figures differ widely between Russian, British and Persian accounts, so none is adopted here.

nodes.label: Sistan arbitrations
nodes.full: Persia and Afghanistan referred their quarrel over the Helmand delta to British arbitration: Major-General Frederic Goldsmid’s 1872 award, ratified in 1873, gave the core of Sistan to Persia and the right-bank lands to Afghanistan, and barred works that would interfere with irrigation on either bank. When the river shifted course the dispute reopened, and Colonel Henry McMahon’s 1903–05 mission re-surveyed the delta and issued a further award in 1905 — the arbitrations to which later Helmand water claims still refer back.
nodes.src: Goldsmid Award (1872, ratified 1873) and McMahon Award (1905), British Indian Foreign Department records on the “Seistan Arbitration” (Qatar Digital Library, File 1880/1904); compare pahlavi-1925-1979::x3 and iran-1979-today::ec3 for the same river’s later treaty and dispute.

nodes.label: Transcaspian Railway reorients Khorasan trade
nodes.full: The Russian Transcaspian Railway reached Ashgabat in 1885 and Samarkand in 1888, running along Khorasan’s northern edge; Mashhad’s trade, once oriented to the Gulf ports and overland routes toward India, increasingly flowed north to Russia, and Russian goods and credit gained ground across north-eastern Persia. British observers such as George Curzon, who travelled the line in 1888–89, tracked the shift as one front of the wider Anglo-Russian contest.
nodes.src: George Curzon, Russia in Central Asia (1889) and Persia and the Persian Question (1892), vol. 1, on Khorasan trade; consular trade reports are the quantitative source and carry their authors’ political interests.

nodes.label: Turkmen raiders and captives
nodes.full: Turkmen alaman raiders seized Persian villagers, pilgrims and soldiers across Khorasan and sold them in the slave markets of Khiva and Bukhara or held them for ransom — a trade recorded by European travellers and Persian officials, and one that left Khorasan’s frontier villages walled and depopulated. Organised raiding largely ended after the Russian conquest of Akhal in 1881; contemporary estimates of captives, often in the tens of thousands, are unreliable and were sometimes used in British and Russian political argument.
nodes.src: George Curzon, Persia and the Persian Question (1892), vol. 1, on the raids and ransoms; Eugene Schuyler, Turkistan (1876), and Arminius Vambery, Travels in Central Asia (1864), on the Central Asian slave markets.

nodes.label: Zand succession crisis
nodes.full: A decade of fratricidal Zand succession disputes opens the way for the Qajar reunification campaign.
nodes.src: background — see the Iran 1722–1789 folio
